name: Linalool
short: Applied to skin: linalool exposed to air forms hydroperoxides, a common cause of contact allergy; 7% to 10% of patients patch-tested for dermatitis reacted, though some reactions may be irritant.
text: Linalool is a fragrance used widely in cosmetics and household products; a review explains that when it is exposed to air it forms oxidation products, of which the hydroperoxides are far stronger skin sensitisers than pure linalool, and another review names linalool and limonene hydroperoxides among the most frequent fragrance sensitisers. In patients patch-tested for suspected contact dermatitis, contact allergy to oxidised linalool was found in 7.0% of 5773 patients (with an increasing trend, and affected patients were younger and predominantly female), positive reactions to linalool hydroperoxides in 8.8% of 5511 consecutive patients, and in 10.1% of 3056 patients in North America, where it was among the most common positive allergens. Several authors caution that many of these reactions were weak, doubtful or irritant, so some positive tests may be false positives. For inhalation, a review of common indoor airborne fragrances found that measured maximum indoor linalool levels were far below the thresholds for sensory irritation of the eyes and upper airways; the abstract does not report inhaled exposure at higher levels. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
